title: Which singularities are physically admissible in finite elasticity?
summary: Finite elasticity can generate both physically meaningful singularities, such as cavitation, and singular weak limits whose physical status is unclear. What criteria distinguish real defect physics from pathological relaxation?

statement.lead: For a finite-elastic body with deformation y and bulk energy E[y], bounded-energy regular sequences can converge weakly to singular limits. The broad target is
equations: \boxed{\text{Which finite-energy singularities are admissible states of a finite-elastic body?}}
E[y]=\int_\Omega W(\nabla y)\,dX\quad\longrightarrow?\quad E_{\rm bulk}[y]+E_{\rm defect}[y]\ \text{or a stronger admissibility constraint}.
statement.after: The canonical unresolved benchmark is three-dimensional neo-Hookean-type energy at W^{1,2}, where regular admissible classes need not be weakly compact and dipole-type singularities can produce a Lavrentiev gap.

why: In finite elasticity the deformation map determines the current geometry, so physical admissibility involves orientation, non-interpenetration, topology, inverse regularity, cavity/surface creation and concentrated energy—not stress alone.
Classical mechanics already accepts some singularities when their physical meaning and defect law are known, as in crack-tip fields and cavitation.

The unresolved issue is how to decide when a singular weak limit should be admitted as a real defect state, supplemented by a defect energy, or rejected as a pathology of an incomplete/overly broad continuum theory.
scope: Primary focus: finite-energy singularities in nonlinear elasticity, with the 3D compressible neo-Hookean-type variational problem as the canonical mathematical benchmark.
Physical singularities such as cavitation, cracks and interfaces are comparison cases; the problem does not assume that one admissibility criterion will cover all singularity classes.

The core is continuum admissibility and energetic completion. Detailed molecular rupture, plasticity and damage may enter as the small-scale physics used to test whether a continuum singularity survives or disappears.

boundary.text: Classical fracture mechanics shows that a singular outer elastic field can remain predictive when it corresponds to a known defect and is supplemented by a fracture law; finite elasticity has its own physically meaningful singular solutions such as cavitation.

The 3D neo-Hookean benchmark sits at critical W^{1,2} regularity, where weak convergence can lose topological/inverse-map information even when local orientation and strong measure-theoretic properties survive.

Conti–De Lellis dipole constructions and subsequent work show concrete lack-of-compactness mechanisms; relaxation theory assigns an explicit singular inverse-map energy to those structures and restores existence in an enlarged class.

Recent injectivity and weak-closure results clarify that the pathology is subtler than simple loss of one-to-one mapping: a.e. injectivity can persist while stronger physical/topological admissibility fails.

A 2026 Lavrentiev result constructs boundary data for which the weakly closed problem achieves strictly lower energy than the regular class through a dipole-type singular mechanism. Enlarging the space and hoping regularity returns therefore cannot solve every loading case.

The remaining mechanics question is broader than the exact neo-Hookean relaxation formula: develop criteria that classify finite-elastic singularities by physical admissibility and determine when bulk elasticity must be completed by defect energy versus stronger kinematic constraints.

settle: For the 3D neo-Hookean benchmark, characterize the relaxed energy and singular defect measures generated by bounded-energy regular sequences, including when the Lavrentiev gap vanishes or is positive.

Provide a physically justified criterion or hierarchy of criteria distinguishing admissible defects from pathological weak limits, and show how it interacts with orientation, injectivity, topology and inverse regularity.
Demonstrate through a resolved small-scale or higher-gradient model whether a disputed singularity survives as a physical defect, acquires a definite defect energy, or is eliminated.

progress.title: Lavrentiev gap makes the regular/relaxed distinction unavoidable
progress.text: Boundary data were constructed for which the weak closure attains strictly lower energy than the regular deformation class through a dipole-type singular mechanism.

progress.title: Weak-limit injectivity and inverse regularity sharpen admissibility
progress.text: Recent results show that weak limits can retain a.e. injectivity and establish existence/inverse regularity in important weakly closed classes, clarifying what information the dipole pathology actually loses.

progress.title: Dipole singularities acquire explicit relaxation energy
progress.text: Relaxation theory identified the dipole structure and introduced a sharp energetic penalty involving the singular part of the inverse deformation.
